import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import colorsys

img = Image.open("barcode.png").convert("RGB")
a = np.array(img)
colmeans = a.mean(axis=0)

# segment into stripes
diffs = np.abs(np.diff(colmeans, axis=0)).sum(axis=1)
boundaries = [0] + [i+1 for i in range(len(diffs)) if diffs[i] > 10] + [len(colmeans)]
segs = []
for i in range(len(boundaries)-1):
    s, e = boundaries[i], boundaries[i+1]
    if e - s < 1: continue
    c = colmeans[s:e].mean(axis=0)
    segs.append((s, e, c))

print("total segments:", len(segs))
h, w = img.size

# Overall palette stats: average color, and hue histogram
avg = colmeans.mean(axis=0)
print("overall avg RGB:", avg.round(1))

hues = []
for s,e,c in segs:
    r,g,b = c/255
    hh,ss,vv = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(r,g,b)
    hues.append((hh*360, ss, vv, vv*255))

hues = np.array(hues)
# categorize
def cat(hdeg, s, v):
    if s < 0.15: return "gray/white/black" if v < 0.9 else ("black/dark" if v < 0.4 else "gray/white")
    if hdeg < 15 or hdeg >= 345: return "red"
    if hdeg < 45: return "orange/brown"
    if hdeg < 70: return "yellow"
    if hdeg < 160: return "green"
    if hdeg < 200: return "cyan"
    if hdeg < 260: return "blue"
    if hdeg < 290: return "purple"
    if hdeg < 320: return "magenta"
    return "pink"

from collections import Counter
cats = Counter()
for hh, ss, vv, _ in hues:
    cats[cat(hh, ss, vv)] += 1
print("hue distribution over stripes (n=%d):" % len(segs))
for k, v in cats.most_common():
    print(f"  {k}: {v} ({100*v/len(segs):.0f}%)")

# Print first 40 stripes as hex
print("\nFirst 20 stripe colors (hex, hue, sat, val):")
for s,e,c in segs[:20]:
    hh,ss,vv = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(*(c/255))
    print(f"  px{s:4d}-{e:4d}  #{int(c[0]):02x}{int(c[1]):02x}{int(c[2]):02x}  h={hh*360:5.1f} s={ss:.2f} v={vv:.2f}")
EOF

import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import colorsys

img = Image.open("barcode.png").convert("RGB")
a = np.array(img)
colmeans = a.mean(axis=0)
diffs = np.abs(np.diff(colmeans, axis=0)).sum(axis=1)
boundaries = [0] + [i+1 for i in range(len(diffs)) if diffs[i] > 10] + [len(colmeans)]
segs = []

    s, e = boundaries[i], boundaries[i+1]
    c = colmeans[s:e].mean(axis=0)
    segs.append((s, e, c))

def show(lo, hi, label):
    print(f"--- stripes {lo}-{hi} ({label}) ---")
    for s,e,c in segs:
        if lo <= s < hi:

# average brightness & saturation overall
vs, ss_ = [], []
for s,e,c in segs:
    hh,ssx,vv = colorsys.rgb_to_hsv(*(c/255))
    vs.append(vv); ss_.append(ssx)
print(f"\nmedian brightness: {np.median(vs):.2f}, median saturation: {np.median(ss_):.2f}")

***Kill This Love*** is the second Korean [extended play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") (third overall) by South Korean girl group [Blackpink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpink "Blackpink"). It was released on April 5, 2019, by [YG Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Entertainment "YG Entertainment") and was distributed through [YG Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Plus "YG Plus") and [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records").[\[3\]](#cite_note-TSN-3) It was their first Korean material since the release of *[Square Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Up "Square Up")* in June 2018, and their first release with [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) [The title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love_\(song\) "Kill This Love (song)") was released as the lead single; it peaked at number two in South Korea and became the first top 50 hit by a female K-pop act in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). The track "[Don't Know What to Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Know_What_to_Do "Don't Know What to Do")" was later promoted on Korean music programs.

*Kill This Love* debuted at number 24 on the US [*Billboard* 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") with 19,200 units sold including over 9,100 [pure sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_sales "Pure sales") moved, making it the highest-charting album by a female K-pop group at the time.[\[5\]](#cite_note-forbes_sales-5) The EP reached the top ten in many territories, including Canada, Japan, New Zealand and South Korea, and the top twenty in Australia. It was certified [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Music_Chart#Certification "Gaon Music Chart") by the [Korea Music Content Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Music_Content_Association "Korea Music Content Association") (KMCA) in June 2019 for selling 250,000 units, becoming Blackpink's second EP to do so after *Square Up*, and was later certified [triple platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Music_Chart#Certification "Gaon Music Chart") in July 2024 for selling 750,000 units.

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

The founder of [YG Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Entertainment "YG Entertainment"), [Yang Hyun-suk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Hyun-suk "Yang Hyun-suk"), announced on February 8, 2019, that Blackpink was scheduled to release an EP in March.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The single and EP were announced on March 25\.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) On March 31 and April 1, multiple individual teaser pictures were posted on Blackpink's social media accounts.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) On July 26, it was announced that the group would release a Japanese version album of the EP through Interscope Records on September 11, 2019\.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The album missed its initial release date and was released on October 16, 2019\.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) A live version of the Japanese version of "Kill This Love", recorded in the [Tokyo Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Dome "Tokyo Dome") on December 4, 2019, was included in the group's third live album *[Blackpink 2019-2020 World Tour In Your Area – Tokyo Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Your_Area_World_Tour#Blackpink_2019–2020_World_Tour_in_Your_Area_–_Tokyo_Dome "In Your Area World Tour")*, released on May 6, 2020, through [Universal Music Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Japan "Universal Music Japan").[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

## Music and lyrics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Music and lyrics")\]

The opening track, "[Kill This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love_\(song\) "Kill This Love (song)")" is a stomping, brassy [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop") track with [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music") elements.[\[12\]](#cite_note-BlackpinkMV-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork_1-13) The song contains "blaring horns and martial percussion",[\[14\]](#cite_note-:0-14) with [Rosé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosé_\(singer\) "Rosé (singer)") and [Jisoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jisoo_\(singer,_born_1995\) "Jisoo (singer, born 1995)") leading the "impassioned" pre-choruses about breaking up.[\[14\]](#cite_note-:0-14) The second track, "Don't Know What To Do" is an [EDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music") and [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") song with throbbing bass, whistle-like hook, and an [acoustic guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_guitar "Acoustic guitar").[\[15\]](#cite_note-Insider-15)[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2)[\[16\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-16) "Kick It", the third song, is a song with elements of Southern trap, synth bass, and acoustic guitar.[\[17\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-17)[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Insider-15) The song is about telling past lovers: “I’m okay being alone / Don’t feel bad for me / I’m going to forget you now.[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2) The fourth track, "Hope Not", is a soft, [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music "Acoustic music") [pop-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-rock "Pop-rock") [balladry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballad "Ballad") about a break-up where the person has moved on from yearning to acceptance.[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2) The closing track, "[Ddu-Du Ddu-Du](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du") (remix)" was described as a "quivering, whomping club-ready Remix".[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2)

## Singles

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Singles")\]

"[Kill This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love_\(song\) "Kill This Love (song)")" was released on April 4, 2019, as the lead single from the [extended play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play").[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) An accompanying music video for the song was directed by Seo Hyun-seung and uploaded onto Blackpink's [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel simultaneously with the single's release. Upon release, the music video broke the record for the most views within 24 hours, accumulating 56\.7 million views.[\[19\]](#cite_note-records-19) Furthermore, it became the fastest video to reach 100 million views on YouTube, doing so in approximately 2 days and 14 hours, beating the record set by fellow Korean artist [Psy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psy "Psy") with "[Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman_\(Psy_song\) "Gentleman (Psy song)")" in 2013\.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) Commercially, the single reached the charts in 27 countries. It peaked at number two in South Korea and became the group's first top-50 hit in the United States and the United Kingdom, thus also becoming the highest-charting female [K-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop "K-pop") song on the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") at the time.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

At Metacritic, which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, the album received a weighted average score of 69 based on 4 reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[\[24\]](#cite_note-MC-24) Laura Dzubay of *[Consequence of Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_of_Sound "Consequence of Sound")* said that the album "functions as a crisper, tighter, and even more badass lunge into the same ideas as last year’s album". She also noted the "balanced production styles, combined with the singers’ talents for vocal elasticity."[\[1\]](#cite_note-CoS-1)

For *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")*, Jeff Benjamin wrote that "There will be time for Blackpink to experiment—ideally in a full-length project. Until then, the women are deepening their brand of K-pop for a quickly growing, language-agnostic fanbase eagerly anticipating every fierce new beat drop."[\[17\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-17) Michelle Kim from *[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")* gave a mixed review, calling the album's production "weirdly dated, like it was crafted earlier in the decade and then forgotten in a time capsule for five years."[\[16\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-16) Rhian Daly of *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")* said that the album "showcases a band who are certainly talented but perhaps not quite ready for the next upward arc in the ride they’re currently on."[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2) Kim Do-heon from *[IZM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IZM "IZM")* gave the EP 2 out of 5 stars, where he criticized the quality of the title track but was more favorable of the group's vocals in "Kick It" and "Hope Not".[\[25\]](#cite_note-izm-25)

The EP was included at number 9 on *[Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_\(magazine\) "Paper (magazine)")*'s list of Top 20 Albums of 2019[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) while "Kick It" was included at number 20 on [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV")'s list of The Best K-pop B-sides of 2019\.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)

***Kill This Love*** is the second Korean [extended play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") (third overall) by South Korean girl group [Blackpink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpink "Blackpink"). It was released on April 5, 2019, by [YG Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Entertainment "YG Entertainment") and was distributed through [YG Plus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Plus "YG Plus") and [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records").[\[3\]](#cite_note-TSN-3) It was their first Korean material since the release of *[Square Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Up "Square Up")* in June 2018, and their first release with [Interscope Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interscope_Records "Interscope Records").[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) [The title track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love_\(song\) "Kill This Love (song)") was released as the lead single; it peaked at number two in South Korea and became the first top 50 hit by a female K-pop act in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") and the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). The track "[Don't Know What to Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Know_What_to_Do "Don't Know What to Do")" was later promoted on Korean music programs.

*Kill This Love* debuted at number 24 on the US [*Billboard* 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") with 19,200 units sold including over 9,100 [pure sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_sales "Pure sales") moved, making it the highest-charting album by a female K-pop group at the time.[\[5\]](#cite_note-forbes_sales-5) The EP reached the top ten in many territories, including Canada, Japan, New Zealand and South Korea, and the top twenty in Australia. It was certified [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Music_Chart#Certification "Gaon Music Chart") by the [Korea Music Content Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Music_Content_Association "Korea Music Content Association") (KMCA) in June 2019 for selling 250,000 units, becoming Blackpink's second EP to do so after *Square Up*, and was later certified [triple platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Music_Chart#Certification "Gaon Music Chart") in July 2024 for selling 750,000 units.

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

The founder of [YG Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YG_Entertainment "YG Entertainment"), [Yang Hyun-suk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Hyun-suk "Yang Hyun-suk"), announced on February 8, 2019, that Blackpink was scheduled to release an EP in March.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) The single and EP were announced on March 25\.[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) On March 31 and April 1, multiple individual teaser pictures were posted on Blackpink's social media accounts.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) On July 26, it was announced that the group would release a Japanese version album of the EP through Interscope Records on September 11, 2019\.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9) The album missed its initial release date and was released on October 16, 2019\.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) A live version of the Japanese version of "Kill This Love", recorded in the [Tokyo Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Dome "Tokyo Dome") on December 4, 2019, was included in the group's third live album *[Blackpink 2019-2020 World Tour In Your Area – Tokyo Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Your_Area_World_Tour#Blackpink_2019–2020_World_Tour_in_Your_Area_–_Tokyo_Dome "In Your Area World Tour")*, released on May 6, 2020, through [Universal Music Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Japan "Universal Music Japan").[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)

## Music and lyrics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Music and lyrics")\]

The opening track, "[Kill This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love_\(song\) "Kill This Love (song)")" is a stomping, brassy [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop") track with [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music") elements.[\[12\]](#cite_note-BlackpinkMV-12)[\[13\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork_1-13) The song contains "blaring horns and martial percussion",[\[14\]](#cite_note-:0-14) with [Rosé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosé_\(singer\) "Rosé (singer)") and [Jisoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jisoo_\(singer,_born_1995\) "Jisoo (singer, born 1995)") leading the "impassioned" pre-choruses about breaking up.[\[14\]](#cite_note-:0-14) The second track, "Don't Know What To Do" is an [EDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music") and [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") song with throbbing bass, whistle-like hook, and an [acoustic guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_guitar "Acoustic guitar").[\[15\]](#cite_note-Insider-15)[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2)[\[16\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-16) "Kick It", the third song, is a song with elements of Southern trap, synth bass, and acoustic guitar.[\[17\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-17)[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2)[\[15\]](#cite_note-Insider-15) The song is about telling past lovers: “I’m okay being alone / Don’t feel bad for me / I’m going to forget you now.[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2) The fourth track, "Hope Not", is a soft, [acoustic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_music "Acoustic music") [pop-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-rock "Pop-rock") [balladry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballad "Ballad") about a break-up where the person has moved on from yearning to acceptance.[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2) The closing track, "[Ddu-Du Ddu-Du](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du") (remix)" was described as a "quivering, whomping club-ready Remix".[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2)

## Singles

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Singles")\]

"[Kill This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love_\(song\) "Kill This Love (song)")" was released on April 4, 2019, as the lead single from the [extended play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play").[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) An accompanying music video for the song was directed by Seo Hyun-seung and uploaded onto Blackpink's [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") channel simultaneously with the single's release. Upon release, the music video broke the record for the most views within 24 hours, accumulating 56\.7 million views.[\[19\]](#cite_note-records-19) Furthermore, it became the fastest video to reach 100 million views on YouTube, doing so in approximately 2 days and 14 hours, beating the record set by fellow Korean artist [Psy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psy "Psy") with "[Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman_\(Psy_song\) "Gentleman (Psy song)")" in 2013\.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) Commercially, the single reached the charts in 27 countries. It peaked at number two in South Korea and became the group's first top-50 hit in the United States and the United Kingdom, thus also becoming the highest-charting female [K-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop "K-pop") song on the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") at the time.[\[21\]](#cite_note-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kill_This_Love&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

Source | Rating

*[Consequence of Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_of_Sound "Consequence of Sound")* | B[\[1\]](#cite_note-CoS-1)

*[IZM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IZM "IZM")* | ![Star](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Star](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Star_empty.svg/20px-Star_empty.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Star_empty.svg/20px-Star_empty.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Star_empty.svg/20px-Star_empty.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[\[25\]](#cite_note-izm-25)

*[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")* | 6\.2/10[\[16\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-16)

*[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* | ![Star](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Star](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Star](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Star_full.svg/20px-Star_full.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![Half star](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Star_half.svg/20px-Star_half.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Star_empty.svg/20px-Star_empty.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[\[17\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-17)

At Metacritic, which assigns a normalized rating out of 100 to reviews from mainstream publications, the album received a weighted average score of 69 based on 4 reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[\[24\]](#cite_note-MC-24) Laura Dzubay of *[Consequence of Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_of_Sound "Consequence of Sound")* said that the album "functions as a crisper, tighter, and even more badass lunge into the same ideas as last year’s album". She also noted the "balanced production styles, combined with the singers’ talents for vocal elasticity."[\[1\]](#cite_note-CoS-1)

For *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")*, Jeff Benjamin wrote that "There will be time for Blackpink to experiment—ideally in a full-length project. Until then, the women are deepening their brand of K-pop for a quickly growing, language-agnostic fanbase eagerly anticipating every fierce new beat drop."[\[17\]](#cite_note-RollingStone-17) Michelle Kim from *[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")* gave a mixed review, calling the album's production "weirdly dated, like it was crafted earlier in the decade and then forgotten in a time capsule for five years."[\[16\]](#cite_note-Pitchfork-16) Rhian Daly of *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")* said that the album "showcases a band who are certainly talented but perhaps not quite ready for the next upward arc in the ride they’re currently on."[\[2\]](#cite_note-NME-2) Kim Do-heon from *[IZM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IZM "IZM")* gave the EP 2 out of 5 stars, where he criticized the quality of the title track but was more favorable of the group's vocals in "Kick It" and "Hope Not".[\[25\]](#cite_note-izm-25)

The EP was included at number 9 on *[Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_\(magazine\) "Paper (magazine)")*'s list of Top 20 Albums of 2019[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) while "Kick It" was included at number 20 on [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV")'s list of The Best K-pop B-sides of 2019\.[\[27\]](#cite_note-27)

Music video

["Ddu-Du Ddu-Du"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IHNzOHi8sJs) on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_video_\(identifier\) "YouTube video (identifier)") ["Ddu-Du Ddu-Du (JP Ver.)"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a1aV8IUgP8Q) on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_video_\(identifier\) "YouTube video (identifier)")

"**Ddu-Du Ddu-Du**" ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 뚜두뚜두; [RR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean"): *Ttuduttudu*) is a song by South Korean girl group [Blackpink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpink "Blackpink"), recorded for their first Korean extended play, *[Square Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Up "Square Up")* (2018). The song was written by YG collaborator [Teddy Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Park "Teddy Park"), while production and composition were handled by Teddy, 24, [Bekuh Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekuh_Boom "Bekuh Boom"), and [R. Tee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Tee "R. Tee"). It was released as the extended play's [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single") to [digital outlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_media "Digital media") on June 15, 2018\. The Japanese version of the single was released through [YGEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YGEX "YGEX") on August 22, 2018, and was distributed in three physical formats. A [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDM_trap_music "EDM trap music") and [pop rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rap "Pop rap") song infused with [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_music "Bubblegum music") and [EDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music") sounds, it uses oriental percussion rhythms and whistling while the title imitates the sound of a gunshot. Its lyrics contain messages of strength and self-assurance.

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" drew generally favorable reviews that complimented its production and the group's performance. It was named the [Song of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_Korea's_Song_of_the_Year "Gallup Korea's Song of the Year") in a public survey conducted by [Gallup Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_Korea "Gallup Korea") in 2018, and appeared on [Melon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melon_\(online_music_service\) "Melon (online music service)") and *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")*'s lists of the best Korean pop songs of all time. It was the top song on the South Korean [Gaon Digital Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Digital_Chart "Circle Digital Chart") for three weeks, Blackpink's second number-one single in the country. It reached number one in Singapore and Malaysia and on the *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* [K-pop Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop_Hot_100 "K-pop Hot 100") and [World Digital Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Digital_Song_Sales "World Digital Song Sales") charts. The song peaked at number 55 on the US [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") and became the first song by a K-pop girl group to enter the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"). It was certified double platinum for streaming and platinum for digital sales in South Korea, platinum in France, Japan and New Zealand, gold in the United States, and silver in the United Kingdom.

An accompanying [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video") features the group members in high-end looks on pink-and-black-hued sets. It became the most-viewed online video by a Korean act within a day of its release, the second-most-watched music video of all time within two days. It is the first music video by a K-pop group to reach two billion views, and remains the most-viewed music video by a K-pop group on YouTube to date. Blackpink promoted "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" with appearances on the [music programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_programs_of_South_Korea "Music programs of South Korea") *[Show! Music Core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show!_Music_Core "Show! Music Core")* and *[Inkigayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkigayo "Inkigayo")* in South Korea. The song's "finger gun" choreography became a dance move. The group sang the song during their [three concert tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Blackpink_live_performances "List of Blackpink live performances"), at California's [Coachella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coachella "Coachella") festival, and the BST [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") festival in London.

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

On June 4, 2018, YG Entertainment confirmed via YG Life that Blackpink would release their debut Korean-language extended play (EP), [*Square Up*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Up_\(EP\) "Square Up (EP)"), on June 15, with "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" serving as its [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single"). It was the group's first original release in a year since "[As If It's Your Last](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As_If_It's_Your_Last "As If It's Your Last")" in June 2017\.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) The odd name was said to be reminiscent of an [onomatopoeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeia "Onomatopoeia").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) Blackpink were quoted as saying, "As it is our debut EP and comeback after one year, we prepared each song with a lot of sincerity and affection." Member [Jennie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennie_\(singer\) "Jennie (singer)") said, "I am confident and I look forward to our comeback. I am happy to be able to express the musicality of Blackpink in various ways."[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was released via [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download") and [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") on June 15, 2018, in conjunction with the release of *Square Up*.[\[4\]](#cite_note-:14-4) It was written and produced by [Teddy Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Park "Teddy Park") and co-produced by Park, [Bekuh Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekuh_Boom "Bekuh Boom"), 24, and [R. Tee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Tee "R. Tee").[\[5\]](#cite_note-:8-5) On August 17, [YGEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YGEX "YGEX") announced that a Japanese version of the track would be released as the group's debut single in Japan on August 22, 2018\. The release featured additional lyrics by Sunny Boy.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) It was subsequently distributed in three physical formats: a CD-only regular edition, a limited edition CD+DVD, and a CD member edition. The regular and limited editions include all the tracks from *Square Up*, in addition to the Japanese version of the single. The limited edition DVD contains behind the scenes footage from the music video as well as a dance practice video. The member edition was packaged as a four-version CD single—one version for each member, and contains only the original version of the track.[\[7\]](#cite_note-ygex-7) On April 5, 2019, a remix of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was included as an album track on Blackpink's second Korean extended play, *[Kill This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love "Kill This Love")*.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

## Composition and lyrics

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Composition and lyrics")\]

![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg/60px-Gnome-mime-sound-openclipart.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)

A sample of the track, showcasing its [EDM trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDM_trap_music "EDM trap music") production with instrumentations of oriental percussion rhythms. The song's title resembles that of a gunshot.

---

*Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media").*

Music journalists have characterized "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" as a "fierce" [pop-rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-rap "Pop-rap") track that "features a prominent [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music") beat" infused with [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_music "Bubblegum music") sounds.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Billboard-10) It combines instrumentations of oriental percussion rhythms and whistling with a trap production.[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-11) Park Bo-ram from [Yonhap News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonhap_News_Agency "Yonhap News Agency") described the single's production as primarily [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music") laced with "aggressive trap" beats,[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) while Im Eun-byel from *[The Korea Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Korea_Herald "The Korea Herald")* noted how the song's title resembled the sound of a gunshot, but also likened it to that of "a spell".[\[13\]](#cite_note-:9-13) Jennie commented how the group reacted when they heard the demo for the song: "When we first listened to the lead track 'Ddu-Du Ddu-Du,' we all thought, 'This is it.'"[\[13\]](#cite_note-:9-13)

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" incorporates the use of trap synths, which is repeated multiple times throughout the first verse. Music producer Azodi commented that its "biggest riff" is already heard in the beginning, "but keeps a lot of space in the verses and chorus for a strong lead vocal line".[\[14\]](#cite_note-:3-14) Its production makes use of percolating [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), while the chorus sees the group members delivering the refrain: "hit you with that 'ddu-du ddu-du'".[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) Azodi observed that, "By the time the chorus is here, you would've heard the hook about four to eight times roughly so it's already been passively drilled into your skull without you realizing".[\[14\]](#cite_note-:3-14) The lyrical content, such as "In my hands is a fat check/ If you're curious, do a fact check", celebrate the members' success.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) In the Japanese rendition, the new English rap verses feature Lisa making references to the character [Patrick Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Star "Patrick Star") from *[SpongeBob SquarePants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpongeBob_SquarePants "SpongeBob SquarePants")* ("Bitch, I’m a star, but no Patrick") and rapper [Ice-T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice-T "Ice-T") ("Like Ice-T, I'm OG"). Jennie’s rap highlights the group's cover of *[GQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ")* [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ"); they were the first female group to have a solo cover shoot ("All my GQ's spread like hummus").[\[19\]](#cite_note-:13-19)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was met with generally favorable reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism"). Hwang Seon-up, a critic from South Korean webzine *[IZM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IZM "IZM")*, awarded the song a 3\.5 out of 5; he noted the unexpected blend of an "ordinary trap beat" with synth instrumentals, which he felt created an "outstanding" climax in the "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" drop.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) Chase McMullen, writing for *[The 405](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_405_\(magazine\) "The 405 (magazine)")*, described the song as both "boisterous" and "beautifully ludicrous", and regarded the chorus to be "essentially nonsense".[\[21\]](#cite_note-The_405-21) He emphasized that "what's being said \[is\] less important than how they say it", and praised the song for its "irresistible cadences" and a seamless flow of verses.[\[21\]](#cite_note-The_405-21) Jeff Benjamin, for *[Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_\(magazine\) "Paper (magazine)")*, commended the song's musical arrangement and placed it at number 13 on their Top 20 K-Pop Songs of 2018 list, remarking that the song perfectly blended "hard hip-hop, honeyed harmonies", and a touch of hazy EDM.[\[22\]](#cite_note-paper-22) Furthermore, Benjamin added, "From the opening shoutout of their group name, Blackpink delivers one of the year's strongest anthems."[\[22\]](#cite_note-paper-22)

Writing for *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")*, Rhian Daly ranked "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" the best song in the group's discography in May 2019, writing, "It's a no-holds-barred, powerful anthem packed full of supreme self-confidence and swagger."[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) She ranked it the 26th best K-pop song of all time in a piece published by *The Forty-Five* in May 2023, remarking that it is rare for K-pop intros to be as recognizable as entrance of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du", and complimented the "perfect combination of rap braggadocio from Jennie and Lisa and powerhouse vocals from Rosé and Jisoo".[\[24\]](#cite_note-:4-24) Taylor Glasby from *[British GQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ")* felt the song embodied the essence of "over the top" K-pop, highlighting the "hooky title refrain", the rappers' sly confidence in the verses, and the emotional build into the chorus that gave the members space to demonstrate their vocal ability.[\[25\]](#cite_note-gq-25) On the other hand, *[Business Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_Insider "Business Insider")*'s Palmer Haasch was not impressed with the song's production, opining that despite its "dramatic" flair and overflowing confidence, the track lacked the "thematic substance" found in songs like "Kill This Love", even though it followed a similar structure.[\[26\]](#cite_note-:10-26) She further noted that the "bridge and final bars don't feel like a particularly satisfying conclusion".[\[26\]](#cite_note-:10-26)

## Commercial performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Commercial performance")\]

In South Korea, "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" debuted at number three on the [Gaon Digital Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Digital_Chart "Circle Digital Chart") for the week of June 16\. The following week, the song ascended to the number one position and scored the highest weekly points in the Gaon Digital Chart.[\[55\]](#cite_note-55) "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" also achieved a [perfect all-kill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_all-kill "Perfect all-kill") upon its release, retaining the status for eleven consecutive days.[\[56\]](#cite_note-56) The song remained atop the Gaon Digital Chart for three weeks and subsequently spent over 50 weeks in the top 100\.[\[57\]](#cite_note-57) It was then certified platinum twice by the [Korea Music Content Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korea_Music_Content_Association "Korea Music Content Association") (KMCA) for accumulating 100 million streams on November 8, 2018, and 2\.5 million digital downloads on April 11, 2019\.[\[58\]](#cite_note-Gaon_Streaming-58)[\[59\]](#cite_note-Gaon_Download-59) Elsewhere in Asia, the song peaked at number one on the digital streaming record charts in Malaysia and Singapore.[\[60\]](#cite_note-mly-60)[\[61\]](#cite_note-rias-61) The Japanese version of the single debuted at number six on the Japanese [Oricon Daily Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oricon_Singles_Chart "Oricon Singles Chart") and peaked at number two six days later, selling 3,725 units.[\[62\]](#cite_note-62)[\[63\]](#cite_note-63) On the chart's weekly issue, the song debuted at number seven with 24,385 physical copies sold.[\[64\]](#cite_note-64) The song was certified platinum in Japan for 100 million streams by the [Recording Industry Association of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_Japan "Recording Industry Association of Japan") (RIAJ) in January 2024\.[\[65\]](#cite_note-RIAJGold-65)

In the United States, "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" debuted and peaked at number 55 on the US [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") on June 30, 2018\. It became the [highest-charting song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_K-pop_songs_on_the_Billboard_charts#Billboard_Hot_100_\(Complete\) "List of K-pop songs on the Billboard charts") by a Korean girl group on the chart, breaking the record previously held by "[Nobody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobody_\(Wonder_Girls_song\) "Nobody (Wonder Girls song)")" by [Wonder Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonder_Girls "Wonder Girls") in 2009\. Within its first week, the song accumulated 12\.4 million streams and sold more than 7,000 digital units in the country.[\[66\]](#cite_note-BBHot100Debut-66) According to [Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminate_\(company\) "Luminate (company)"), the song received 113 million [on-demand streams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") in 2018\.[\[67\]](#cite_note-67) On August 23, 2019, the song was certified gold by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA), for track equivalent sales of 500,000 units in the US, making Blackpink the first Korean girl group and third Korean artist overall to receive the certification, after [Psy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psy "Psy") and [BTS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BTS "BTS").[\[68\]](#cite_note-RIAA-68)[\[69\]](#cite_note-69) In Canada, "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" debuted at number 22 on the [Canadian Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Hot_100 "Canadian Hot 100") and remained on the chart for ten weeks.[\[70\]](#cite_note-CANHOT100-70) In Europe, the song peaked at number 32 on the [Scottish Singles and Albums Charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Singles_and_Albums_Charts "Scottish Singles and Albums Charts")[\[71\]](#cite_note-SCOOCC-71) and number 78 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"), making Blackpink the first K-pop girl group in history to enter the chart.[\[72\]](#cite_note-72) The track reached 45\.5 million streams in the United Kingdom as of September 2022, becoming the group's most-streamed song in the country.[\[73\]](#cite_note-73)[\[74\]](#cite_note-74) In June 2021, the song was awarded a silver [certification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification") in the country by the [British Phonographic Industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Phonographic_Industry "British Phonographic Industry") (BPI) for track-equivalent sales of 200,000 units.[\[75\]](#cite_note-UK_Cert-75)

## Music video

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Music video")\]

[![Jennie sitting atop a diamond-encrusted tank on the set of the music video](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/52/Blackpink_-_Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du_%28music_video_screenshot%29.jpg/250px-Blackpink_-_Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du_%28music_video_screenshot%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Blackpink_-_Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du_\(music_video_screenshot\).jpg)

A scene in the music video where Jennie raps while sitting on a diamond-encrusted [T-34-85 tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-34 "T-34").

The music video for "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was uploaded to the group's official YouTube channel along with the release of *Square Up* on June 15\.[\[76\]](#cite_note-76) It soon became the most viewed online video in the first 24 hours by a Korean act, and the second most watched [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video") of all time with more than 36\.2 million views within 24 hours after release, surpassing Psy's "[Gentleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentleman_\(Psy_song\) "Gentleman (Psy song)")" (2013) and second only to [Taylor Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylor_Swift "Taylor Swift")'s "[Look What You Made Me Do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Look_What_You_Made_Me_Do "Look What You Made Me Do")" (2017).[\[77\]](#cite_note-Billboard2018Jul5-77) The music video hit 100 million views in 10 days, making "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" the only music video by an all-female K-pop group to achieve the feat within the timeframe.[\[78\]](#cite_note-78) In November 2018, five months after release, it became the fastest music video by a K-pop group to reach 500 million views and the fifth most viewed K-pop video of all time.[\[79\]](#cite_note-79) A dance practice video for the song was released on June 18, 2018\.[\[80\]](#cite_note-80)

The track's music video primarily focuses on the choreography and features the group in high-end looks amid pink-and-black-hued sets.[\[81\]](#cite_note-81)[\[82\]](#cite_note-:7-82) It depicts the group members with a variety of props and attires; Jennie appears as a queen on a chessboard and is seen sitting atop a diamond-encrusted tank with shopping bags.[\[83\]](#cite_note-83) Lisa disperses a burst of smoke resembling a pair of wings, before she is seen with a pink [cockatoo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockatoo "Cockatoo") and a [katana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katana "Katana"). Rosé looks up towards another version of herself on a pedestal dressed in glimmering gown, while at one point, she is seen swinging on a chandelier. Jisoo appears sporting a pink wig while standing in front of a mural depicting herself, and is surrounded by a crowd of masked men all capturing the mural with their mobile phones.[\[84\]](#cite_note-:6-84) She initially stands unnoticed due to the wig she is wearing, however, the crowd begins to take notice and record her every move after she stumbles and falls while walking.[\[84\]](#cite_note-:6-84) Explaining the concept behind the scene, Jisoo elaborated: "The message is about how people can go crazy about the celebrity figures and how they will aim at the celebrities if they make mistakes. We wanted to portray a scene which is interesting and meaningful to us."[\[82\]](#cite_note-:7-82)

Writing for the July 2018 issue of *Seoul Magazine*, Kristina Manente expressed appreciation for the song's blend of traditional Korean instrumentals with the beat and bass of hip-hop, describing it as an "auditory delight". Manente wrote that the fusion was reflected in the music video through its integration of elements from Korean architecture, and observed a recurring trend in South Korean music videos where traditional and contemporary elements are blended together, in which she thought contributed to their unique charm.[\[85\]](#cite_note-85) *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* named it the eighth best music video of 2018, describing it as "a feat of bonkers, maximalist creativity that includes the best use of a tank in a music video since [Master P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_P "Master P")'s "[Make 'Em Say Uhh!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make_'Em_Say_Uhh! "Make 'Em Say Uhh!")" in 1998\.[\[30\]](#cite_note-RS_Video-30) Blackpink later revealed that the "gun-shooting hand gesture", featured during the chorus in the music video, was not included in the initial choreography; Jennie explained that the original move involved the members extending their arms, with palms facing downwards, while swaying their hands from side to side. The group altered the dance move to the gun-shooting gesture on the day of the music video shoot.[\[86\]](#cite_note-86)

In October 2018, "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" won Best Dance Video at the [2018 MTV Video Music Awards Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_MTV_Video_Music_Awards_Japan "2018 MTV Video Music Awards Japan").[\[39\]](#cite_note-:11-39) [YouTube Rewind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_Rewind "YouTube Rewind") named it the second most popular music video in South Korea during 2018, only behind "[Love Scenario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_Scenario "Love Scenario")" by label-mate [iKon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IKon "IKon").[\[87\]](#cite_note-:5-87) On January 21, 2019, the video became the most-viewed music video by a K-pop group on YouTube, with 620\.9 million views; the video averaged 2\.5 million views per day since its release, with 1\.95 million daily views in January 2019\.[\[88\]](#cite_note-Ddu_Views-88) On November 11, 2019, the music video surpassed one billion views, making Blackpink the first K-pop group, second girl group, and fourth music group overall to achieve the milestone.[\[89\]](#cite_note-89) The video subsequently surpassed two billion views on January 4, 2023, making it the first K-pop group video to achieve the milestone, after "[Gangnam Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gangnam_Style_\(music_video\) "Gangnam Style (music video)")" (2012) by Psy.[\[90\]](#cite_note-90)

## Live performances and other usage

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Live performances and other usage")\]

As part of promotions for *Square Up*, Blackpink premiered the song on live television along with "[Forever Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forever_Young_\(Blackpink_song\) "Forever Young (Blackpink song)")" on *[Show! Music Core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show!_Music_Core "Show! Music Core")* on June 16, 2018\. *Osen* contrasted the "refreshing and melodic" performance of "Forever Young" with the strong hip-hop concept of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du".[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-11) They subsequently appeared on *Inkigayo* for the first time to perform the song the next day.[\[91\]](#cite_note-91) On June 22, the group was slated to perform the track at the [Lotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotte_Corporation "Lotte Corporation") Duty Free Family Concert 2018; however after several songs, their performance was abruptly halted before having a chance to perform "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" due to safety concerns. Fans expressed discontent regarding the handling of the situation as many in the audience paid tickets to see the group and they did not return after being escorted off the stage. The event organizers soon apologized for the incident.[\[92\]](#cite_note-92)

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was used as the opening number for the group's first two headlining concert tours, the [Blackpink Arena Tour 2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpink_Arena_Tour_2018 "Blackpink Arena Tour 2018") and the [In Your Area World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Your_Area_World_Tour "In Your Area World Tour") (2018–2020).[\[93\]](#cite_note-93)[\[94\]](#cite_note-94) They also performed the song at the TGC Kitakyushu 2018 festival by [Tokyo Girls Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Girls_Collection "Tokyo Girls Collection") in Japan on October 6,[\[95\]](#cite_note-95) and the SBS Super Concert in [Suwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suwon "Suwon") on October 14\.[\[96\]](#cite_note-96) At year-end award ceremonies and festivals, Blackpink performed the song live at the [2018 Melon Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Melon_Music_Awards "2018 Melon Music Awards") on December 1, where they won the award for best female dance performance.[\[97\]](#cite_note-97)[\[98\]](#cite_note-98) On December 25, Jennie performed her single "[Solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solo_\(Jennie_song\) "Solo (Jennie song)")" at the annual *[SBS Gayo Daejeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_Gayo_Daejeon "SBS Gayo Daejeon")*, before reuniting with the rest of the members for the performance of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" and "Forever Young".[\[99\]](#cite_note-99) The following month, the group made performances with the song at the [33rd Golden Disc Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/33rd_Golden_Disc_Awards "33rd Golden Disc Awards") on January 5, 2019,[\[100\]](#cite_note-100) and the 8th [Gaon Chart Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaon_Chart_Music_Awards "Gaon Chart Music Awards") on January 23\.[\[101\]](#cite_note-101)

[![Blackpink performing onstage](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/BLACKPINK_Pink_Venom_Tour_2022_%2852543715107%29.jpg/250px-BLACKPINK_Pink_Venom_Tour_2022_%2852543715107%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BLACKPINK_Pink_Venom_Tour_2022_\(52543715107\).jpg)

Blackpink performing the song during the [Born Pink World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_Pink_World_Tour "Born Pink World Tour") in London, 2022

On February 9, 2019, the group performed in the United States for the first time at Universal Music's Grammy Artist Showcase with "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" and "Forever Young".[\[102\]](#cite_note-102) Two days later, Blackpink made their American television debut in New York City on *[The Late Show with Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Late_Show_with_Stephen_Colbert "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert");* their performance on the show coincided with the 55th anniversary of [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' American television debut at [the same theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Sullivan_Theater "Ed Sullivan Theater").[\[103\]](#cite_note-103) They also made a performance with the song on *[Good Morning America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Morning_America "Good Morning America")* the following day.[\[104\]](#cite_note-104) At the April 2019 [Coachella Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coachella_Valley_Music_and_Arts_Festival "Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival") in Indio, California, "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was also used for Blackpink's opening performance.[\[105\]](#cite_note-105) On January 31, 2021, the group performed the song as part of their [set list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_list "Set list") for their virtual concert [The Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Show_\(concert\) "The Show (concert)"); the stage was decorated with a display of fire and pyrotechnics and was transformed into a shallow pool. Maddy Myer from *[Teen Vogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_Vogue "Teen Vogue")* wrote that the performance was "one of the greatest spectacles of the concert".[\[106\]](#cite_note-106) Matthew Mohan-Hickson from *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* noted how "the fire and water elements shine" and deemed it one of the concert's standout moments.[\[107\]](#cite_note-107) "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was also included in the set list for the group's second world tour, the [Born Pink World Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_Pink_World_Tour "Born Pink World Tour") (2022–2023).[\[108\]](#cite_note-108)

In 2018, "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was added to the soundtrack of the dance rhythm game *[Just Dance 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Dance_2019 "Just Dance 2019").*[\[109\]](#cite_note-109) The song was featured in the fourth episode of season three of [Freeform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeform_\(TV_channel\) "Freeform (TV channel)") series *[The Bold Type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bold_Type "The Bold Type")* in April 2019, and the fifth episode of the [tvN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TvN_\(South_Korean_TV_channel\) "TvN (South Korean TV channel)") television series *[Mr. Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Queen "Mr. Queen")* in December 2020\.[\[110\]](#cite_note-110)[\[111\]](#cite_note-111) South Korean boy band [Stray Kids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stray_Kids "Stray Kids") performed "God's Ddu-Du Ddu-Du", a *[Deadpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadpool_\(film\) "Deadpool (film)")*\-themed mashup of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" with their own song "[God's Menu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God's_Menu "God's Menu")", during the 2021 Mnet competition show *[Kingdom: Legendary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom:_Legendary_War "Kingdom: Legendary War")*.[\[112\]](#cite_note-112) In November 2023, members of the British royal band performed a cover of "Ddu-Du-Ddu-Du" at the gates of London's [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") in recognition of the group members receiving honorary [MBEs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") from [King Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_III "Charles III").[\[113\]](#cite_note-113)

## Impact and legacy

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Impact and legacy")\]

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was named the [Song of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_Korea's_Song_of_the_Year "Gallup Korea's Song of the Year") in the 2018 edition of the annual public survey conducted by South Korean research company [Gallup Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_Korea "Gallup Korea").[\[114\]](#cite_note-114)*The Korea Herald* reported that the "gun-shooting hand gesture" helped make "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" the most-covered K-pop song in 2018\.[\[115\]](#cite_note-115) In December 2019, *British GQ* named it among the best K-pop songs of the 2010s and the highlight work of the genre from 2018\.[\[25\]](#cite_note-gq-25) Lucy Ford, from the same publication, said the song helped Blackpink cement "the badass, empowered 'girl crush' concept" initially propelled by [2NE1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2NE1 "2NE1").[\[116\]](#cite_note-116) Writing for *[Sisa Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisa_Journal "Sisa Journal")*, music critic [Kim Young-dae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Young-dae_\(critic\) "Kim Young-dae (critic)") wrote that the song and choreography underscored Blackpink's "sophisticated and edgy image" among girl groups.[\[117\]](#cite_note-117)

In 2021, a panel of 35 music experts curated by Melon and newspaper *[Seoul Shinmun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul_Shinmun "Seoul Shinmun")* ranked "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" 13th in the top 100 K-pop songs.[\[28\]](#cite_note-:1-28) [KBS Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Broadcasting_System "Korean Broadcasting System") director Soyeon Kang wrote that the song, characterized by its EDM trap beats and strong hooks, established Blackpink's musical identity and helped the group capture worldwide attention and break record.[\[118\]](#cite_note-:12-118) In 2023, *Rolling Stone* ranked it sixth among Korean pop songs, saying it helped perfect K-pop's "EDM trap template" and elevate it to "global heights".[\[31\]](#cite_note-:2-31)

Music video

["Ddu-Du Ddu-Du"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IHNzOHi8sJs) on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_video_\(identifier\) "YouTube video (identifier)") ["Ddu-Du Ddu-Du (JP Ver.)"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a1aV8IUgP8Q) on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_video_\(identifier\) "YouTube video (identifier)")

"**Ddu-Du Ddu-Du**" ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language "Korean language"): 뚜두뚜두; [RR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revised_Romanization_of_Korean "Revised Romanization of Korean"): *Ttuduttudu*) is a song by South Korean girl group [Blackpink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackpink "Blackpink"), recorded for their first Korean extended play, *[Square Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Up "Square Up")* (2018). The song was written by YG collaborator [Teddy Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Park "Teddy Park"), while production and composition were handled by Teddy, 24, [Bekuh Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekuh_Boom "Bekuh Boom"), and [R. Tee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Tee "R. Tee"). It was released as the extended play's [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single") to [digital outlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_media "Digital media") on June 15, 2018\. The Japanese version of the single was released through [YGEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YGEX "YGEX") on August 22, 2018, and was distributed in three physical formats. A [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDM_trap_music "EDM trap music") and [pop rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_rap "Pop rap") song infused with [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_music "Bubblegum music") and [EDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music") sounds, it uses oriental percussion rhythms and whistling while the title imitates the sound of a gunshot. Its lyrics contain messages of strength and self-assurance.

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" drew generally favorable reviews that complimented its production and the group's performance. It was named the [Song of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_Korea's_Song_of_the_Year "Gallup Korea's Song of the Year") in a public survey conducted by [Gallup Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_Korea "Gallup Korea") in 2018, and appeared on [Melon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melon_\(online_music_service\) "Melon (online music service)") and *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")*'s lists of the best Korean pop songs of all time. It was the top song on the South Korean [Gaon Digital Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circle_Digital_Chart "Circle Digital Chart") for three weeks, Blackpink's second number-one single in the country. It reached number one in Singapore and Malaysia and on the *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")* [K-pop Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop_Hot_100 "K-pop Hot 100") and [World Digital Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Digital_Song_Sales "World Digital Song Sales") charts. The song peaked at number 55 on the US [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") and became the first song by a K-pop girl group to enter the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"). It was certified double platinum for streaming and platinum for digital sales in South Korea, platinum in France, Japan and New Zealand, gold in the United States, and silver in the United Kingdom.

An accompanying [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video") features the group members in high-end looks on pink-and-black-hued sets. It became the most-viewed online video by a Korean act within a day of its release, the second-most-watched music video of all time within two days. It is the first music video by a K-pop group to reach two billion views, and remains the most-viewed music video by a K-pop group on YouTube to date. Blackpink promoted "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" with appearances on the [music programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_programs_of_South_Korea "Music programs of South Korea") *[Show! Music Core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show!_Music_Core "Show! Music Core")* and *[Inkigayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inkigayo "Inkigayo")* in South Korea. The song's "finger gun" choreography became a dance move. The group sang the song during their [three concert tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Blackpink_live_performances "List of Blackpink live performances"), at California's [Coachella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coachella "Coachella") festival, and the BST [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London") festival in London.

## Background and release

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background and release")\]

On June 4, 2018, YG Entertainment confirmed via YG Life that Blackpink would release their debut Korean-language extended play (EP), [*Square Up*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_Up_\(EP\) "Square Up (EP)"), on June 15, with "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" serving as its [lead single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lead_single "Lead single"). It was the group's first original release in a year since "[As If It's Your Last](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/As_If_It's_Your_Last "As If It's Your Last")" in June 2017\.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) The odd name was said to be reminiscent of an [onomatopoeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeia "Onomatopoeia").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) Blackpink were quoted as saying, "As it is our debut EP and comeback after one year, we prepared each song with a lot of sincerity and affection." Member [Jennie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennie_\(singer\) "Jennie (singer)") said, "I am confident and I look forward to our comeback. I am happy to be able to express the musicality of Blackpink in various ways."[\[3\]](#cite_note-3)

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was released via [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download") and [streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_media "Streaming media") on June 15, 2018, in conjunction with the release of *Square Up*.[\[4\]](#cite_note-:14-4) It was written and produced by [Teddy Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Park "Teddy Park") and co-produced by Park, [Bekuh Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekuh_Boom "Bekuh Boom"), 24, and [R. Tee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Tee "R. Tee").[\[5\]](#cite_note-:8-5) On August 17, [YGEX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YGEX "YGEX") announced that a Japanese version of the track would be released as the group's debut single in Japan on August 22, 2018\. The release featured additional lyrics by Sunny Boy.[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) It was subsequently distributed in three physical formats: a CD-only regular edition, a limited edition CD+DVD, and a CD member edition. The regular and limited editions include all the tracks from *Square Up*, in addition to the Japanese version of the single. The limited edition DVD contains behind the scenes footage from the music video as well as a dance practice video. The member edition was packaged as a four-version CD single—one version for each member, and contains only the original version of the track.[\[7\]](#cite_note-ygex-7) On April 5, 2019, a remix of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was included as an album track on Blackpink's second Korean extended play, *[Kill This Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kill_This_Love "Kill This Love")*.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8)

Music journalists have characterized "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" as a "fierce" [pop-rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-rap "Pop-rap") track that "features a prominent [trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trap_music "Trap music") beat" infused with [bubblegum pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_music "Bubblegum music") sounds.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-Billboard-10) It combines instrumentations of oriental percussion rhythms and whistling with a trap production.[\[11\]](#cite_note-:0-11) Park Bo-ram from [Yonhap News Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonhap_News_Agency "Yonhap News Agency") described the single's production as primarily [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music") laced with "aggressive trap" beats,[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) while Im Eun-byel from *[The Korea Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Korea_Herald "The Korea Herald")* noted how the song's title resembled the sound of a gunshot, but also likened it to that of "a spell".[\[13\]](#cite_note-:9-13) Jennie commented how the group reacted when they heard the demo for the song: "When we first listened to the lead track 'Ddu-Du Ddu-Du,' we all thought, 'This is it.'"[\[13\]](#cite_note-:9-13)

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" incorporates the use of trap synths, which is repeated multiple times throughout the first verse. Music producer Azodi commented that its "biggest riff" is already heard in the beginning, "but keeps a lot of space in the verses and chorus for a strong lead vocal line".[\[14\]](#cite_note-:3-14) Its production makes use of percolating [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer"), while the chorus sees the group members delivering the refrain: "hit you with that 'ddu-du ddu-du'".[\[15\]](#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) Azodi observed that, "By the time the chorus is here, you would've heard the hook about four to eight times roughly so it's already been passively drilled into your skull without you realizing".[\[14\]](#cite_note-:3-14) The lyrical content, such as "In my hands is a fat check/ If you're curious, do a fact check", celebrate the members' success.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) In the Japanese rendition, the new English rap verses feature Lisa making references to the character [Patrick Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Star "Patrick Star") from *[SpongeBob SquarePants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpongeBob_SquarePants "SpongeBob SquarePants")* ("Bitch, I’m a star, but no Patrick") and rapper [Ice-T](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice-T "Ice-T") ("Like Ice-T, I'm OG"). Jennie’s rap highlights the group's cover of *[GQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ")* [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ"); they were the first female group to have a solo cover shoot ("All my GQ's spread like hummus").[\[19\]](#cite_note-:13-19)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ddu-Du_Ddu-Du&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

"Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" was met with generally favorable reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism"). Hwang Seon-up, a critic from South Korean webzine *[IZM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IZM "IZM")*, awarded the song a 3\.5 out of 5; he noted the unexpected blend of an "ordinary trap beat" with synth instrumentals, which he felt created an "outstanding" climax in the "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" drop.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) Chase McMullen, writing for *[The 405](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_405_\(magazine\) "The 405 (magazine)")*, described the song as both "boisterous" and "beautifully ludicrous", and regarded the chorus to be "essentially nonsense".[\[21\]](#cite_note-The_405-21) He emphasized that "what's being said \[is\] less important than how they say it", and praised the song for its "irresistible cadences" and a seamless flow of verses.[\[21\]](#cite_note-The_405-21) Jeff Benjamin, for *[Paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_\(magazine\) "Paper (magazine)")*, commended the song's musical arrangement and placed it at number 13 on their Top 20 K-Pop Songs of 2018 list, remarking that the song perfectly blended "hard hip-hop, honeyed harmonies", and a touch of hazy EDM.[\[22\]](#cite_note-paper-22) Furthermore, Benjamin added, "From the opening shoutout of their group name, Blackpink delivers one of the year's strongest anthems."[\[22\]](#cite_note-paper-22)

Writing for *[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")*, Rhian Daly ranked "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du" the best song in the group's discography in May 2019, writing, "It's a no-holds-barred, powerful anthem packed full of supreme self-confidence and swagger."[\[23\]](#cite_note-23) She ranked it the 26th best K-pop song of all time in a piece published by *The Forty-Five* in May 2023, remarking that it is rare for K-pop intros to be as recognizable as entrance of "Ddu-Du Ddu-Du", and complimented the "perfect combination of rap braggadocio from Jennie and Lisa and powerhouse vocals from Rosé and Jisoo".[\[24\]](#cite_note-:4-24) Taylor Glasby from *[British GQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ "GQ")* felt the song embodied the essence of "over the top" K-pop, highlighting the "hooky title refrain", the rappers' sly confidence in the verses, and the emotional build into the chorus that gave the members space to demonstrate their vocal ability.[\[25\]](#cite_note-gq-25) On the other hand, *[Business Insider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_Insider "Business Insider")*'s Palmer Haasch was not impressed with the song's production, opining that despite its "dramatic" flair and overflowing confidence, the track lacked the "thematic substance" found in songs like "Kill This Love", even though it followed a similar structure.[\[26\]](#cite_note-:10-26) She further noted that the "bridge and final bars don't feel like a particularly satisfying conclusion".[\[26\]](#cite_note-:10-26)
